title: Fifty-two letters
hook: Guru Arjan's long acrostic on the letters, a school for the soul (Gauri, ang 250)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Guru Ram Das: a routine, a city, and songs of longing. Your line was the fourth guru's way.

A, apple. B, ball. C, cat. The alphabet chart on a classroom wall sticks a picture to each letter, and some of those pictures never quite come unstuck. Now aim that schoolroom trick somewhere else. Each letter opens a short lesson, not about apples or cats, but about the mind, the ego, death, grace, and the Name. That's what Guru Arjan, Guru Ram Das's son, did in a long hymn in Raga Gauri. Its name tells you what it is: Bavan Akhri.
screen: `A, APPLE. B, BALL.` → `EACH LETTER, A LESSON.` → `GURU ARJAN, IN GAURI.`

segments.voice: Bavan Akhri: fifty-two letters, the hymn's own title. It's an acrostic: stanza after stanza begins on a letter, and the letter becomes the doorway into a teaching. A school for the soul, with the alphabet as its timetable. But before the first letter there's a salok, and it tells you who the teacher is. Paraphrased: the Divine Guru is mother, the Divine Guru is father, the Divine Guru is master and the Transcendent Lord. The Guru is companion, the destroyer of ignorance, kin and brother. So this school begins with a relationship, not a lesson. The teacher is also a parent, a friend, the one who stays. Then the letters come. And this path has been circling letters a long time. In the first year we heard young Nanak asking his village teacher what the letters really pointed to. We heard the tradition of Guru Angad shaping the Gurmukhi letters so ordinary people could read the hymns. We heard the Japji say that through letters the Name is spoken and praise is sung. The Bavan Akhri stands in that line. Letters, for the Gurus, aren't only for contracts and shopping lists. They're a way to the Name, if you learn them for what they point to. That's the quiet point of an acrostic: letter after letter gets its turn, and each is taught to point the same way.
screen: `BAVAN AKHRI: FIFTY-TWO LETTERS.` · `FIRST, THE TEACHER: MOTHER, FATHER.` · `THE LETTERS AGAIN, ON THIS PATH.` · `THE WHOLE ALPHABET POINTS ONE WAY.` · then, large: `A SCHOOL FOR THE SOUL.`

segments.voice: Hold the first letter of your own name in your mind, the way a child traces it on a slate. Let it carry one lesson worth living by, patience if it's P, kindness if it's K, taking the first good one that comes rather than searching hard. If you pray, say Waheguru as you trace it.
Bavan Akhri. Fifty-two letters: Guru Arjan's acrostic in Raga Gauri, where each letter opens a lesson and the Guru is the teacher. Today's word.
Your line: the letters again. Every letter can be taught to point toward the Name. Twelve hundred days, and counting.

howItsDone: Sikhs read and study the Bavan Akhri in the Guru Granth Sahib, and its opening salok, on the Guru as mother and father, is recited and sung in Sikh prayer and kirtan.

chat.says: Why would a Guru write a hymn that goes through the alphabet?
options: Each letter opens a lesson, so the whole alphabet points one way: toward the Name.
To teach children spelling, since the hymn is mainly a writing exercise.
To show that only scholars who know every letter can ever reach God.
